title: General Microbiology (MCB 201)
description: Microbial structure, growth, sterilisation and disinfection, bacterial genetics and an introduction to viruses, fungi and immunity.

topics.title: History and Bacterial Cell Structure
topics.summary: Pioneers of microbiology, prokaryotic structure, Gram staining and bacterial shapes.

notes.b: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first observed microbes with simple microscopes. Louis Pasteur disproved spontaneous generation (swan-neck flask), developed pasteurisation and vaccines against rabies and anthrax. Robert Koch established Koch's postulates linking a specific microbe to a disease and identified the causes of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera. Joseph Lister introduced antiseptic surgery with carbolic acid; Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin (1928).

Bacteria have a cell wall of peptidoglycan. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer with teichoic acids and stain purple (retain crystal violet–iodine); Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) and stain pink/red (counterstained with safranin). Gram stain steps: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol/acetone decolouriser → safranin. Other structures: capsule (antiphagocytic), flagella (motility), pili/fimbriae (adhesion; sex pili for conjugation) and endospores (resistant resting forms in Bacillus and Clostridium). Shapes: cocci, bacilli, spirilla; arrangements such as chains (streptococci) and clusters (staphylococci). Mycobacteria have mycolic acids and need acid-fast (Ziehl–Neelsen) staining.

topics.title: Microbial Growth and Culture Media
topics.summary: Bacterial growth curve, oxygen and temperature requirements, and types of culture media.

notes.b: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission. The growth curve in a closed culture has four phases: lag (adaptation, no increase in number), log/exponential (fastest division; most sensitive to antibiotics), stationary (nutrient exhaustion, growth equals death) and decline/death. Generation time of E. coli is about 20 minutes. By oxygen requirement: obligate aerobes (M. tuberculosis, Pseudomonas), obligate anaerobes (Clostridium, Bacteroides), facultative anaerobes (E. coli, Staphylococcus), microaerophiles (Campylobacter, Helicobacter). By temperature: psychrophiles, mesophiles (most human pathogens, optimum ~37 °C) and thermophiles.

Basal media (nutrient agar) support non-fastidious organisms. Enriched media (blood agar, chocolate agar for Haemophilus and Neisseria) support fastidious organisms. Selective media inhibit unwanted organisms: MacConkey (Gram-negative enterics), Lowenstein–Jensen (mycobacteria), Thiosulphate–citrate–bile salts–sucrose (TCBS) for Vibrio cholerae, Sabouraud dextrose agar for fungi. Differential media distinguish organisms: MacConkey differentiates lactose fermenters (pink: E. coli, Klebsiella) from non-fermenters (pale: Salmonella, Shigella); blood agar shows haemolysis (α partial/green, β complete, γ none).

topics.title: Sterilisation and Disinfection
topics.summary: Physical and chemical methods of controlling microbes and their uses in health care.

notes.b: Sterilisation destroys all microorganisms including spores; disinfection destroys most pathogens but not necessarily spores (on inanimate objects); antisepsis applies chemicals to living tissue. Moist heat is the most reliable method: autoclaving at 121 °C, 15 psi for 15–20 minutes kills spores (checked with Bacillus stearothermophilus / Geobacillus indicators). Dry heat (hot-air oven, 160 °C for 2 hours) sterilises glassware and powders. Incineration destroys contaminated waste. Pasteurisation (63 °C for 30 min or 72 °C for 15 s) reduces milk-borne pathogens. Filtration (0.22 µm) sterilises heat-labile solutions; ionising radiation (gamma rays) sterilises disposable syringes.
k: Sterilisation kills spores; disinfection may not

notes.b: Alcohols (70% ethanol or isopropanol) are effective skin antiseptics (70% works better than absolute alcohol because water aids protein denaturation). Chlorine compounds (sodium hypochlorite/bleach, 0.5% for spills) are broad-spectrum disinfectants. Iodine and povidone-iodine are antiseptics. Chlorhexidine is used for hand hygiene and surgical skin preparation. Glutaraldehyde (2%) is a high-level disinfectant ('cold sterilant') for endoscopes. Phenolics and hydrogen peroxide are also used. Prions are highly resistant to standard methods.

topics.title: Bacterial Genetics and Antimicrobial Resistance
topics.summary: Mutation, gene transfer, plasmids and mechanisms of antibiotic resistance.

notes.b: Bacteria have a single circular chromosome and often plasmids (extrachromosomal DNA carrying resistance or toxin genes). Genetic variation arises by mutation and by horizontal gene transfer: transformation (uptake of free DNA — Griffith's experiment with Streptococcus pneumoniae), transduction (transfer by bacteriophages) and conjugation (transfer through a sex pilus, often of plasmids such as R factors). Transposons ('jumping genes') move between DNA sites.

Resistance mechanisms include enzymatic inactivation (β-lactamases, extended-spectrum β-lactamases, carbapenemases), altered targets (altered penicillin-binding protein PBP2a in MRSA), reduced permeability, and efflux pumps. Misuse of antibiotics — self-medication, incomplete courses, use in livestock and over-the-counter sales — drives resistance, a major public health threat in Nigeria. Antimicrobial stewardship promotes the right drug, dose and duration.
k: Misuse drives resistance; stewardship limits it

topics.title: Viruses, Fungi and Protozoa: An Introduction
topics.summary: Viral structure and replication, fungal forms, and medically important protozoa.

notes.b: Viruses are acellular obligate intracellular parasites containing either DNA or RNA (never both) within a protein capsid; some have a lipid envelope derived from the host membrane (enveloped viruses are more easily inactivated by detergents and alcohol). Replication steps: attachment, penetration, uncoating, synthesis of nucleic acid and proteins, assembly and release. Retroviruses such as HIV use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA. Viruses are not affected by antibacterial antibiotics; they are grown in cell culture, embryonated eggs or animals, not on agar. Bacteriophages infect bacteria.
k: Viruses: DNA or RNA, never both
Grown in cell culture, not agar

notes.b: Fungi are eukaryotes with chitin cell walls and ergosterol in their membranes (the target of azoles and amphotericin B). Yeasts are unicellular (Candida, Cryptococcus); moulds form hyphae (Aspergillus, dermatophytes causing ringworm/tinea); dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma) are moulds at room temperature and yeasts at body temperature. Protozoa are unicellular eukaryotes: Plasmodium (malaria, transmitted by female Anopheles), Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery, liver abscess), Giardia lamblia (malabsorptive diarrhoea), Trypanosoma brucei (sleeping sickness, tsetse fly), Leishmania (sandfly) and Trichomonas vaginalis (sexually transmitted).
